The Power of the Kill Shot
2027 Big Ten Data Viz • NCAA WBB (2020–2026)
Measuring "Spurtability" in Women's College Basketball

What is a Kill Shot—and Why Does It Win Games?

In basketball, few moments shift momentum faster than an unanswered scoring spree. Inspired by analyst Evan Miyakawa's "Kill Shot" framework (EvanMiya.com), a Kill Shot is defined as any 10–0 (or larger) unanswered scoring run. Teams that frequently generate Kill Shots can erase deficits in minutes, while teams that prevent them protect leads and avoid upsets.

This dashboard adapts Miyakawa's Men's Basketball framework to NCAA Women's Basketball (2020–2026) across 76,000+ team-game performances. Use the interactive timeline below to explore how every Division 1 program falls into four spurtability profiles, or use the top navigation bar to explore Predicted Success, The W-Husky (31-0+ runs), and our Data & Methodology.

Strong (Bottom-Right)

Scores lots of 10-0 runs while rarely giving them up. Home of title contenders.

Streaky (Top-Right)

High-volatility teams that trade big runs both ways. Dangerous underdogs.

Least Streaky (Bottom-Left)

Low-run, methodical games. Reliable with a lead, but hard to mount quick comebacks.

Suspect (Top-Left)

Prone to giving up big runs without the firepower to answer back.

Predicting Game & Season Outcomes

Quarters vs. Halves: How Game Format Shapes the Kill Shot

One of the biggest structural differences between NCAA Women's and Men's Basketball is the clock: the women's game is played in four 10-minute quarters (with built-in quarter breaks and team fouls resetting every 10 minutes), while the men's game is played in two 20-minute halves. Those extra quarter breaks act as natural momentum stoppers—giving opposing coaches free timeouts to draw up a play and halt a scoring drought. Yet as the data below reveals, when a WBB team does break through those stoppages to post a 10–0 Kill Shot, it is an even stronger predictor of victory than in the men's game—outperforming Evan Miyakawa's MBB benchmarks across every single run tier.

Data & Methodology

This project was built for the 2027 Big Ten Academic Alliance Data Viz Championship. Below is a full breakdown of our data sources, cleaning pipeline, run-extraction algorithm, and statistical models.

1. Data Sources & Citations

  • NCAA WBB Play-by-Play & Team Box Scores: Sourced from the official competition dataset via the SportsDataverse / wehoop pipeline (derived from ESPN JSON feeds).
  • Kill Shot Framework & MBB Benchmarks: Inspired by Evan Miyakawa's "The Power of The 10-0 Run" (EvanMiya.com, March 15, 2023).
  • 2026 Final AP Top 10: Sourced from College Basketball at Sports Reference.
  • Team Logos: Dynamically loaded via ESPN's public NCAA team logo CDN using SportsDataverse team IDs.

2. Why 2020–2026?

While the raw dataset extends back to 2006, an audit of play-by-play completeness revealed a sharp coverage threshold starting in the 2019–2020 season:

  • 2017–2019: Only ~1,540–1,578 games/season had granular play-by-play events logged (~515k events/yr).
  • 2020–2026: Coverage expanded to 4,947–6,011 games/season (1.65M–2.82M events/yr).
  • Filtering to 2020–2026 and requiring a minimum of 15 games played ensures unbiased season medians and accurate quadrant classifications.

3. Scoreboard-Delta Run Extraction

Raw play-by-play logs occasionally contain missed shots with non-zero score_value fields, string-sorted sequence numbers, or misattributed team_id values. To guarantee 100% accurate scoring runs, our pipeline uses a scoreboard-delta method:

  1. Sort every game's events chronologically by period_number, cumulative home_score + away_score, and numeric play sequence.
  2. Compute exact row-to-row increments in home_score and away_score, keeping only valid basketball scoring increments (1–4 points where exactly one team's score increases).
  3. Group consecutive scoring plays by the same team into unanswered runs and classify milestones: Kill Shot (10-0+), Avalanche (20-0+), Husky (30-0+), and W-Husky (31-0+).

4. Quadrant Definitions

Each team-season is classified relative to its specific season's D1 median for Kill Shots Scored per game and Kill Shots Conceded per game (dashed lines on the scatterplot):

  • Strong: Above-median For, Below-median Conceded.
  • Streaky: Above-median For, Above-median Conceded.
  • Least Streaky: Below-median For, Below-median Conceded.
  • Suspect: Below-median For, Above-median Conceded.

5. Predictive Models

  • In-Game Win Probability (Logistic Regression): Fit via scikit-learn on all 2020–2026 team-games using three features: kill_shots_for, kill_shots_against, and max_run_for.
  • Season-Long Predictor (Linear Regression): Ordinary least squares regression predicting overall season Win % from season-long Kill Shot Margin per game (Kill Shots For/Gm − Kill Shots Conceded/Gm).
